title: Daily Eval Briefing 2026-11-02: Thin Same-Day Signal, Custom Code Benches, and Harness Token Accounting
subtitle: Fresh coverage is mostly 2026-11-01 through 2026-10-31: private-repo code benches, typed-decision protocols, and inspect_ai harness controls dominate over new public leaderboard shocks.
summary: Same-day publishable coverage for 2026-11-02 is thin; the strongest evaluation signals sit in the prior 36 hours and soft 72-hour window. The clearest methodological shift is toward organization-owned code benchmarks that score agents on private repositories rather than static public suites, raising contamination control while tightening harness and token-accounting requirements. Parallel forum and guide material emphasize typed decision protocols, open submission rules, and careful interpretation of LLM, agent, and RAG scorecards. Inspect AI’s late-October release and follow-on test hygiene changes further underline that conversation rewriting, compaction resets, and monitor token budgets are now first-class reproducibility surfaces. Researchers and infra teams should treat harness configuration and hidden prompt cost as part of the reported result, not as invisible scaffolding.
key_takeaways: Treat private-repo code benches (repo2bench/Harbor-style) as anti-leakage infrastructure: gains are only comparable when harness, tools, and optimization loops are versioned and disclosed.
Typed-decision and multilingual submission protocols matter because they constrain judge ambiguity; open evaluation guides beat opaque leaderboard deltas when same-day news is sparse.
Agent harnesses hide tokens—system prompts, tool schemas, compaction, and monitor models—so cost and context budgets must be reported alongside accuracy.
Inspect AI 0.3.287 (2026-10-31) makes runtime conversation rewrite and compaction reset() explicit; any before/after comparison without pinning that release is weakly reproducible.
Practical benchmark guides are useful for taxonomy, not for claiming new capability frontiers; separate what a suite measures from what a marketing score implies.
body_en:
Official daily briefing for 2026-11-02 (Europe/Istanbul). Same-day primary coverage is thin: no dense cluster of brand-new arXiv eval papers or arena shocks landed on the report day itself in the provided set. The publishable signal is therefore drawn from the freshest technical items in the last ~36 hours and the soft 72-hour tail, with dates called out explicitly. The through-line is evaluation quality under private tasks, harness opacity, and protocol documentation rather than a single headline leaderboard move.

Custom code evaluation as an Eval Factory
On 2026-11-01, Google Cloud Community published “Build your own custom code benchmark,” framing Software Factory needs as Eval Factory needs: benchmark coding agents on your own repository with repo2bench and Harbor, then optimize with Harness-squared tooling. For evaluation research, the important claim is not another public coding score. It is that validity increasingly depends on tasks that never entered pretraining corpora in the first place. Public SWE-style suites remain useful for coarse ranking, but they are chronically exposed to contamination, mirror leakage, and training-time overfitting. A private-repo bench flips the default: the task distribution is owned by the organization, ground truth is the repo’s tests and acceptance criteria, and leakage risk drops if the corpus is truly held out.

That flip creates new comparability constraints. Once every lab builds its own suite, cross-lab numbers stop being interchangeable. Infra teams must version the repo snapshot, the harness (tool allowlists, timeouts, sandbox image, retrieval settings), the agent loop, and any Harness-squared optimization that rewrites prompts or scaffolding between runs. Without that bundle, a reported “+12% on our internal coding bench” is an uncontrolled before/after. The Medium piece’s practical implication for researchers is to publish harness manifests alongside scores, and for infra teams to treat benchmark generation pipelines as production systems with release tags, not ad-hoc scripts.

Typed decision protocols and open submission rules
Also on 2026-11-01, a Hugging Face Forums post announced a PT-BR typed-decision benchmark covering twelve external models with an open evaluation and submission guide. Even with a thin abstract in the feed, the methodological signal is clear: typed decisions reduce free-form judge drift by forcing structured outputs and explicit decision classes, and an open submission guide is itself an evaluation artifact. Multilingual typed tasks further stress whether English-centric rubrics and judges transfer. For stakeholders, the takeaway is protocol surface area: who can submit, how runs are packaged, what fields are required, and how ties or invalid types are scored. Those rules often move rankings more than model weights.

When same-day news is sparse, open guides and typed protocols are higher-value than rumor about anonymous arena swings. They give infra a checklist: schema validation before scoring, rejection policies for malformed outputs, and documented model lists so external twelve-model comparisons can be audited. Leakage still matters—if typed items or answer keys circulate in training data, structure alone will not save validity—but typed formats at least make automated integrity checks cheaper.

Hidden tokens as a first-class harness metric
A 2026-11-01 OpenAI Community thread titled “The hidden tokens in your agent harness” points at a chronic reproducibility failure mode. Agent evaluations frequently report task success while omitting the token mass of system instructions, tool definitions, memory dumps, retrieved chunks, compaction summaries, and secondary monitor models. Those hidden tokens change effective context length, latency, cost, and sometimes behavior when the model is near context limits. Two runs that look identical in task prompt can differ dramatically once harness overhead is counted.

For evaluation quality, this is not a billing footnote. It is a construct-validity issue. If Model A “wins” only because the harness silently truncates history for Model B, or because a monitor model consumes budget that Model A never paid, the comparison is confounded. Practical implication: report input/output tokens for the candidate, plus harness overhead and any monitor or judge model tokens, as separate line items. Prefer harnesses that expose those counters rather than burying them in SDK defaults.

Inspect AI: conversation rewrite, compaction reset, and scorer hygiene
The Inspect AI release v0.3.287 is dated 2026-10-31 (within the soft freshness window) and remains operationally relevant on 2026-11-02 because many teams pin Inspect for agent and sentinel-style evals. The release notes highlight that a runtime can hold and rewrite a react() conversation at turn boundaries, and that compaction handlers gain reset(). Separately, sentinel host behavior surfaces input budget and the token count of a monitor model—an unusually direct alignment with the “hidden tokens” theme from the community forum. Registry reservation for range_goal types is a smaller but real compatibility surface for anyone extending Inspect with custom goals.

A follow-on commit on 2026-11-01 tightened test isolation: a score-state test now uses a task name no other test registers. That is not a user-facing feature, but it signals where reproducibility bugs hide—shared registries and colliding task names that make scorer tests flake or falsely pass. Infra teams upgrading through 0.3.287 should re-baseline any multi-turn agent evals that depend on compaction or conversation rewrite semantics, and confirm sentinel/monitor token accounting matches their reporting templates. Holding model weights fixed while changing Inspect minor versions can still move measured trajectories.

Benchmark literacy versus new evidence
Two Medium evaluation pieces sit in the window: “A Practical Guide to LLM, Agent, and RAG Benchmarks” (2026-11-01) and “Top 50 AI & LLM Evaluation Interview Questions and Answers for 2027” (2026-10-31). Neither should be read as empirical breakthroughs. They matter as orientation for teams that must choose metrics under pressure. The practical guide’s framing—what suites measure, how they are scored, and what results actually tell us—is the right antidote to treating every leaderboard delta as capability news. Agent and RAG benches especially mix retrieval quality, tool reliability, and generation quality; collapsing them into a single percentage invites false conclusions about model upgrades.

The interview-question roundup is secondary signal: useful for vocabulary alignment inside hiring and onboarding, weak as a source of methodological novelty. Mention it only as soft-window context that industry attention remains on fundamentals—contamination, judge bias, metric choice—rather than on a single new public suite.

What not to overweight
Several OpenAlex items appear in the feed but are off-focus for LLM evaluation methodology: knowledge-graph application notes with a future-dated stamp, mining multi-agent operational architecture, and Scotland just-transition policy monitoring. They are not used here as evidence of LLM benchmark change. Discipline on this point matters on thin days: filling space with adjacent “AI” titles would invent a news cycle the corpus does not support.

Synthesis for researchers and infra
The freshest meaningful eval shift around this briefing is compositional: private custom code benches plus explicit harness and token accounting, reinforced by Inspect’s conversation-rewrite and monitor-budget features, and steadied by typed-decision and open-submission protocol work. On a thin same-day calendar, that composition is the story. Teams should (1) prefer held-out organizational tasks when claiming coding-agent gains, (2) publish harness and token manifests, (3) pin evaluation-framework versions when comparing multi-turn agents, and (4) demand typed or otherwise constrained decision formats when using judges or model routers. None of these items alone rewrites the field; together they raise the bar for what counts as a comparable, contamination-aware, reproducible evaluation result going into the next reporting day.
methodology_risks:
Comparability risk is elevated when organizations adopt private repo2bench-style suites without publishing harness manifests. Scores become locally meaningful and globally incomparable; silent Harness-squared optimization between runs can masquerade as model improvement. Cross-paper or cross-vendor claims that omit repo snapshot hashes, tool policies, and framework versions should be treated as non-comparable.

Leakage and judge-drift risks remain asymmetric. Private tasks reduce public-web contamination but do not eliminate internal leakage through issue trackers, CI logs, or employee fine-tuning corpora. Typed-decision benchmarks reduce free-form judge variance only if schemas are enforced and invalid outputs are scored consistently; otherwise judges reintroduce subjectivity at the margins. Multilingual PT-BR settings add transfer risk if English rubrics or English-tuned judges are reused without calibration.

Harness opacity is the dominant confounder in this window. Hidden tokens from tools, compaction, and monitor models change effective budgets and can truncate differently across providers. Inspect’s conversation rewrite and compaction reset() features (v0.3.287, 2026-10-31) mean that identical task definitions can yield non-identical trajectories across framework versions. Any longitudinal dashboard that does not pin Inspect (or equivalent) releases and report monitor/candidate token splits risks mistaking harness drift for capability change.
